verdict.reasoning: Patient reports not having much appetite and energy and feeling down: "not having much of an appetite and energy lately" and "I've been feeling down and I didn't really have energy"; duration is described as "Started long, long ago" and later as months.

Decreased appetite linked to job change with duration 3–3.5 months: "That must have started when I changed over to the new law firm. I would say months ago" and then specifies "Three months ago. Three and a half months ago."

Weight loss amount and duration: "Have you lost any weight?" / "I have a little bit"; duration about 6 months: doctor suggests "Roughly six months. Would you say" and patient replies "Something like that?"; amount: "Oh, gosh, I would say less than a stone."
Intermittent nausea: patient states "I feel nauseous. Every now and again. It's coming up. Yeah, Just every now and again."
Headaches reported at work: "I have trouble at work sometimes. Having headaches, feeling nauseous."

Shortness of breath with palpitations in lift: "Just shortness of breath... when I go into the lift... my heart starts beating and I can't really breathe" and clinician clarifies palpitations: "You're describing, like, palpitations to me" and patient agrees "Yeah."
Denies cough: "You also mentioned that you're feeling short of breathing... Is there any cough?" / Patient: "No, not really. Just shortness of breath."
Denies chest pain: "Do you get any chest pains with it?" / Patient: "Not really, no." and clinician repeats "Okay. No chest pain." / Patient: "No chest pain."

Normal bowels but going less often: "How are your bowels?" / Patient: "That's okay. I would say I don't really have problems when going to the toilet. It's to spend less." indicating decreased frequency likely from reduced intake.
Denies diarrhea: clinician asks "you don't have any diarrhea?" / Patient: "No, no diarrhea? No."
Denies blood/mucus in stool: "there's no blood in the poo? No mucus, nothing of that sort?"; patient responds "No, no, just."
Denies vomiting: "You mentioned nausea. Have you been ever sick with it?" / Patient: "No, actually not." (no vomiting).
Denies reflux: "Do you suffer from acid reflux?" / Patient: "I do not, no."
Clinician posits ability to walk a mile without SOB: "So you can walk about a mile. And you don't feel short of breath at all?" / Patient: "That's right, yes."

Later, exertional tolerance is said to be unclear due to minimal walking: patient later says "I haven't been walking lately at all... it's, like, really hard for me to identify when I feel the shortness of breath."
Sexual concerns via wife's complaints: "My wife was starting to complain as well in nightly activities."
No recent labs: "When was your last blood test?" / Patient: "Haven't taken one in a long time."
History of hypothyroidism: "I had too little activity of my thyroid" and clinician clarifies "Oh, yeah. Underactive thyroid? Yes."

Previously on thyroxine, stopped around time of law‑firm change: "And in that I took thyroxine." then "Are you using it every day?" / "Not anymore." / "I have not been taking it in the last. Actually, since I changed law firm, I would say." The law‑firm change was dated to 3–3.5 months earlier.

Occupation and firm change timing: patient jokes "Who likes to be a lawyer?" then affirms job; earlier he ties appetite change to "when I changed over to the new law firm" and specifies "Three months ago. Three and a half months ago."

Constitutional symptoms: fatigue/low energy ("I didn't really have energy"; "you're not having the umph"), decreased appetite ("loss of appetite"), low mood ("I've been feeling down"), and unintentional weight loss <1 stone over about 6 months are all documented.

Episodic SOB with palpitations in lift without chest pain or cough, exertional tolerance uncertain: symptoms in lift and palpitations described, patient denies cough and chest pain; later notes "I haven't been walking lately at all... hard... to identify when I feel the shortness of breath," making exertional capacity unclear.

Hypothyroidism with stopped thyroxine about 3–3.5 months ago and no recent TFTs: history of underactive thyroid, previously on thyroxine, stopped since law‑firm change (~3–3.5 months), and "Haven't taken [a blood test] in a long time."

Intermittent nausea, otherwise stable bowels, no GI red flags: nausea "every now and again"; bowels "okay" but less frequent; denies diarrhea, blood, mucus, and vomiting, matching absence of red‑flag GI symptoms.
Headaches are part of the assessment: patient reports "Having headaches" at work; thus inclusion as an assessed symptom is supported.
Sexual concerns: "My wife was starting to complain as well in nightly activities" indicates concerns around sexual activity; decreased function is implied by complaint.

Plan for broad blood tests: clinician says "we'll just do a general set of bloods where we look at things like anemia, how your kidney functions are, your livers, all that with vitamin levels" and in context of hypothyroid, thyroid tests are implicitly included; listing TSH/T4 is a direct clinical inference.
Plan to review labs then examine if normal: "after we get those set of bloods, we will find out if we can find anything in them. If that's all clear, then we would need to do a physical examination."
A&E advice for palpitations or chest pain: "Obviously with palpitations or chest pain, if you get. That's more of a medical emergency, you need to go to A and E for that."
Advice to contact clinic if new bowel changes or vomiting: "if your, you know, bowels change or you're being sick again, you need to get in touch with us."
Advice to seek care if feeling worse: "If you're feeling poorly, don't wait for that. Just get in touch with us again."
Call support via app using 0300 number: "you need to ring up support... there's a number on your app... It's an O300 number. So just call that number."
Clinician will submit lab request form: "now you need to ring up support and I'll do the form for you."
Results trigger text to book follow-up: "once you get the result, you will receive a text message through your phone to tell you to book an appointment."

Follow-up after labs prompted by text: same statement—"you will receive a text message... to tell you to book an appointment"—indicates follow-up will be arranged after blood test results via text prompt.
